messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Manaia was fifty-six years old, a detective who had spent thirty years walking into rooms where other people had done terrible things. He was divorced, living alone in a small house near the coast, and he had come to therapy because he could no longer sleep without drinking himself into a stupor. What he remembered—what he could not stop remembering—was the smell of burnt kerosene and the feel of his father’s hand closing around his wrist when he was eight years old. His father had been a fisherman, a man who drank and who believed that fear made boys strong. The abuse had not been constant, but it had been predictable: the smell of the kerosene heater, the sound of the front door opening late, the way his father’s voice would drop into something quiet and deliberate before the first blow. Manaia had learned to read the signs. He had also learned that when he tried to explain any of this to anyone—his mother, a teacher, a social worker who visited once—the thread of the story would slip from his hands. He would stammer, lose the sequence, and end up standing in silence while the other person looked at him with pity or disbelief. He had come to believe that this proved something about him: that he was a lousy coper, that the event had happened to him because of the sort of person he was. These beliefs had settled into him the way dust settles into a room that no one cleans. They were not thoughts he examined. They were the air he breathed.

The past did not stay in the past. Something in his surroundings—a flicker of light, the sound of a heavy door closing—could instantly bring back the full memory without warning, and when it did, the rage that flooded him was so dense and immediate that he had once punched a hole in his own kitchen wall. He had been standing at the stove, and the burner had clicked on, and for a moment the smell of gas had been the smell of kerosene, and then he was eight years old again and his father was in the room. The memory did not arrive as a story. It arrived as a body state: heart hammering, hands shaking, a heat in his chest that demanded action. Manaia had learned to manage these moments by detaching himself from the memories, pushing them away before they could fully form. He had also learned to avoid people altogether. He had stopped going to the station bar after shifts. He had stopped answering calls from his sister. He had stopped wearing button-down shirts because the fabric reminded him of the shirt his father had worn the night he broke Manaia’s collarbone. The avoidance worked, for a while. But it had a cost. His captain had noticed his absences. His colleagues had stopped inviting him to case reviews. He had become the detective who worked alone, the one who took the cold cases nobody else wanted because they required no collaboration, no small talk, no risk of someone touching his shoulder from behind.

The hypervigilance was constant. He could not fall asleep without checking the locks three times, without positioning himself so that he could see the bedroom door. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, and when he did sleep, he woke at the smallest sound—a floorboard creaking, the refrigerator kicking on—and his heart would be pounding before he knew why. He had come to believe that the world was not safe, that it had never been safe, and that his reactions since the event—the rage, the avoidance, the sleeplessness—only confirmed what he already knew: that he was not the kind of person who could handle things. This belief looped back on itself. The more he avoided people, the more isolated he became, and the more isolated he became, the more convinced he was that he was fundamentally broken. He had tried, once, to tell a therapist about the abuse. He had sat in the chair, opened his mouth, and lost the thread entirely. He had left after fifteen minutes and never gone back.

What finally brought him in was a case. A missing boy, twelve years old, from a family that lived near the docks. The boy’s father was a fisherman. Manaia had walked into the house and smelled kerosene, and for a moment he had been unable to move. The memory had hit him without warning: his father’s hand, the smell, the cold linoleum floor. He had excused himself, gone to the bathroom, and stood with his hands gripping the sink while the rage built and then subsided. He had finished the interview. He had found the boy three days later, alive, hiding in a friend’s shed. But the experience had shaken something loose. He had gone home that night and sat in the dark, and he had understood, for the first time, that he could not keep doing this alone. He was afraid of what he might do the next time the rage came. He was afraid of what he had already become.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph conveys that triggers (e.g., flicker of light, sound of a door) directly cause or lead to maladaptive strategies (avoidance, detachment); triggers bring back memory, but the strategies are described as separate responses.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: Memory → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the memory itself directly causes or leads to negative appraisals; the negative beliefs are described as longstanding and not explicitly caused by the memory.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory causes or leads to triggers; triggers are described as external stimuli that evoke the memory, not the reverse.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat causes or leads to negative appraisals; the threat is described as constant, but the causal link to appraisals is absent.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat causes or leads to triggers; triggers are described as external cues, not as a result of threat.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, detachment) cause or lead to the memory; the strategies are used to manage the memory, not to produce it.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to negative appraisals; the appraisals are described as pre-existing or reinforced by isolation, not by the strategies themselves.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to triggers; triggers are described as external stimuli independent of the strategies.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Something in his surroundings—a flicker of light, the sound of a heavy door closing—could instantly bring back the full memory without warning, and when it did, the rage that flooded him was so dense and immediate that he had once punched a hole in his own kitchen wall.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After these episodes, he started taking the long way home from the station, adding forty minutes to his drive, because the route that passed the docks—the smell of salt and diesel—was the fastest way to bring it all back.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had come to believe that this proved something about him: that he was a lousy coper, that the event had happened to him because of the sort of person he was.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
And each time the memory surfaced unbidden—the smell of kerosene, the feel of his father's hand—he felt that belief harden into something more certain, as though the intrusion itself was proof that he could not move past it.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had been standing at the stove, and the burner had clicked on, and for a moment the smell of gas had been the smell of kerosene, and then he was eight years old again and his father was in the room.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After that memory broke through, he began noticing the smell of gas everywhere—in the station's break room, in a neighbor's barbecue, in the exhaust of a passing truck—each one a new thread pulling him back toward that kitchen.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The hypervigilance was constant. He could not fall asleep without checking the locks three times, without positioning himself so that he could see the bedroom door.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This unrelenting sense of danger had quietly convinced him that his life was permanently reduced—that he was no longer the person who could sit with his back to a room or walk through a doorway without scanning for exits.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The hypervigilance was constant. He could not fall asleep without checking the locks three times, without positioning himself so that he could see the bedroom door.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living at that pitch of alertness, he found that the ordinary sounds of his own house—the creak of a floorboard, the hum of the refrigerator—had become signals he could not ignore, each one demanding his full attention.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had also learned to avoid people altogether. He had stopped going to the station bar after shifts.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
But the longer he avoided it—the longer he refused to speak about the memory or let himself feel it fully—the more it seemed to press against the edges of his awareness, waiting for the moment his guard dropped.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had learned to manage these moments by detaching himself from the memories, pushing them away before they could fully form.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After three years of this—of pushing it down, of turning away from his sister's calls, of refusing to let the memory take shape—he had started to believe that he was a weaker man than his father had ever been, because his father had never needed to run from his own past.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had also learned to avoid people altogether. He had stopped going to the station bar after shifts.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
And each place he avoided—the bar, the docks, the street where his sister lived—became its own kind of trigger, a landmark in the geography of what he could not face.
<<<END>>>
